UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                            BEFORE THE
                  FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION
Reliability Technical Conference                                                    Docket No. AD26-8-000


         PRE-TECHNICAL CONFERENCE REMARKS OF DR. VARUN SIVARAM
                                    ON BEHALF OF
                                   EMERALD AI, INC.


Panel 1: The State of Reliability in a Changing Energy Landscape
    I.    Introduction

Chairman and Commissioners, thank you for the opportunity to participate in the Reliability
Technical Conference and discuss how the rapid growth of large loads, particularly data centers,
can be accomplished while continuing to ensure the reliability and affordability of our nation’s
power system.

My name is Varun Sivaram, and I am the Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Emerald AI, a
technology company transforming AI data centers into flexible resources that support the
reliability and stability of the electric grid. Emerald AI enables data centers to dynamically adjust
their electricity demand by orchestrating computing workloads and on-site energy equipment at
data centers, strengthening grid reliability while maintaining strict computing performance
standards. Enabling data centers to operate flexibly could unlock 100 gigawatts from the existing
power system.1 In addition, flexibility can accelerate AI innovation and U.S. leadership while
enabling affordability and reliability for communities across the country. Flexible AI data centers
can serve as good citizens to power grids and to local communities by operating in ways that
strengthen, rather than strain, the electric power system.2 Greater utilization of existing
infrastructure can deliver meaningful affordability benefits for electricity customers. According

Potential for Integration of Large Flexible Loads in US Power Systems,” Nicholas Institute for Energy, Environment
& Sustainability, Duke University (Feb. 2025).
https://nicholasinstitute.duke.edu/sites/default/files/publications/rethinking-load-growth.pdf
2
 Baglino, D., V. Troy, M. Polsky, and V. Sivaram. “3 Principles to Make AI Data Centers Good Grid Citizens,”

 to an analysis by the Brattle Group, a 10 percent improvement in grid utilization could reduce
average electricity rates by approximately 3.4 percent.3

These principles have also brought together a broader coalition of industry participants. Emerald
AI, Google, and NVIDIA founded the AI Energy Management Alliance (AEMA), a first-of-its-
kind coalition bringing together leaders across the AI and energy sectors to advance flexible AI
data centers that operate as good grid citizens.4 AEMA champions technology-neutral,
performance-based policies that recognize and reward flexible data centers capable of adjusting
their electricity demand during periods of grid stress, enabling expedited interconnection while
protecting grid reliability and affordability for American households and communities.5

The United States is experiencing extraordinary growth in electricity demand, driven in
significant part by the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure. This growth presents an important
challenge for utilities and grid operators seeking to accommodate substantial new loads while
preserving system reliability and protecting ratepayers. New generation and transmission
infrastructure will remain essential to meeting this demand. At the same time, improvements in
how large loads consume electricity can help make more efficient use of the infrastructure
already available.

Historically, the power system has been planned for data centers as inflexible loads, requiring
infrastructure sufficient to serve their maximum anticipated demand, including during periods of
peak system stress. Modern AI data centers can operate differently. Through advances in
computing hardware, workload orchestration, and on-site energy management, these facilities
can adjust their demand in response to grid conditions, providing utilities and grid operators with
an additional resource to maintain reliability.

Rarely does the nation have an opportunity to accomplish all of its goals at the same time:
advances in AI innovation, economic growth, and competitiveness; affordability for
communities; and reliability for the grid. But it will take decisive action by policymakers at the
federal, state, and local levels to seize this triple win and unlock the nation’s power system for
AI data centers and other sources of demand and economic growth. A grand bargain would offer
larger and faster power connections, as well as reduced rates, to AI data centers that verifiably
and enforceably provide flexibility as good citizens to curb costs and advance reliability.

     II.   Flexible AI Data Centers Support Grid Reliability

Load flexibility includes the capability of a large load customer to reduce, shift, or defer
electricity consumption in response to a utility or system operator signal while maintaining the
customer’s operational or service-level requirements. (In these remarks, I focus on flexibility on
timescales spanning several hours to tens of seconds, which is critical for unlocking capacity,
better utilizing the power system, and providing relief during periods of peak grid stress.
Separately, large loads can also advance reliability by controlling their transient fluctuations in
power demand, performing low-voltage ride-through, etc., which are also important and distinct
capabilities.)

AI data centers are particularly well-suited to provide this flexibility because not all
computational workloads require the same level of uninterrupted power consumption or
immediate completion. Certain workloads can be shifted, deferred, or temporarily slowed
without compromising critical computing functions. These capabilities can also be coordinated
with other sources of flexibility, such as on-site batteries, generation, and cooling systems, to
provide additional flexibility. To be sure, AI workloads and AI hardware are extremely valuable
and expensive, so the flexibility of AI data centers should not be overused; however, AI data
centers can provide substantial flexibility while at the same time ensuring that mission-critical
computational work continues at peak performance, with 18-55% flexibility for AI workloads
that still meet customer performance needs reported in the scientific literature.6

This software-defined approach enables data centers to adjust the power consumed by AI
workloads themselves, providing flexibility independently of on-site batteries or generation.
Computational flexibility can also complement onsite energy technologies, enabling data centers
to coordinate multiple sources of flexibility (from computations, batteries, etc.) to respond to grid
signals and meet defined power targets while protecting priority workloads.

As utilities and grid operators plan for the rapid growth of large, energy-intensive loads, it is
important that interconnection and transmission planning processes account for the actual
operating capabilities of modern AI data centers. Historically, these processes have treated large
loads as static and inflexible, without recognizing their ability to adjust electricity consumption
during periods of grid stress. Incorporating proven load flexibility capabilities into planning
assumptions would allow utilities and grid operators to better assess the capacity available to
accommodate new demand while ensuring reliability and improving affordability. Data centers
can commit to dispatchability within defined operating limits, supported by transparent telemetry
and enforceable performance requirements. Recognizing these capabilities in interconnection


6

Power Consumption Flexibility of AI Data Centers for Demand Response Participation. The 17th ACM

 studies and operational planning can enable faster and larger grid connections, reduce the need
for costly infrastructure upgrades, and make better use of the grid infrastructure we already have.

The potential reliability benefits are significant. During periods of grid stress, transmission and
generation resources may operate near their limits, reducing the system's ability to accommodate
equipment failures, supply disruptions, or other contingencies. Flexible data centers can
temporarily reduce consumption during these periods, easing pressure on the grid and providing
operators with an additional tool to maintain supply-demand balance. This capability can help
reduce the risk of involuntary service interruptions, including brownouts and blackouts, while
mitigating the reliability risks associated with rapid demand growth.

Equally important, flexibility can allow utilities and grid operators to plan for the actual
operating characteristics of large loads rather than assuming that every facility will require its
maximum requested power at all times. Where demand reductions are sufficiently predictable,
verifiable, and enforceable, they can be incorporated into system planning and operational
requirements.

III.     Real-World Demonstrations of AI Flexibility

AI flexibility has been proven under real-world operating conditions through a series of
demonstrations involving Emerald AI, electric utilities, grid operators, and leading technology
providers.7 Emerald AI has now conducted smaller-scale six demonstrations at commercial data
centers around the world, deployed flexibility software at multi-MW, full data center scale, and
is preparing with partners such as NVIDIA and Digital Realty to launch an AI data center of
roughly 100 MW in Virginia that will be power-flexible.

In Phoenix, Arizona, Emerald AI partnered with Oracle, NVIDIA, Salt River Project, and the
Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) to demonstrate flexibility on a commercial AI
computing cluster. The demonstration showed that the cluster could sustain a 25 percent
reduction in electricity consumption for three hours while maintaining quality-of-service
requirements for customer AI workloads.8 The results were subsequently published in the peer-
reviewed scientific journal Nature Energy, providing evidence that AI workloads can respond
predictably to utility-defined power requirements without disrupting priority computing
operations.9

 Emerald AI subsequently conducted the United Kingdom’s first live demonstration of a power-
flexible AI factory with National Grid, EPRI, NVIDIA, and Nebius, showcasing how AI
workloads can dynamically adjust power consumption in response to grid conditions while
preserving critical computing performance.10 Over five days, the system responded to 22 live
dispatch events, including unexpected signals with no advance notice.11 The demonstration
achieved sub-minute response times, including a 30 percent power reduction in under 40
seconds, and sustained demand reductions ranging from 10 to 40 percent for periods of up to 10
hours.12 Throughout these events, the system maintained service requirements for high-priority
computing workloads (see Appendix, Exhibit B).

In addition, Emerald AI has collaborated with NVIDIA, EPRI, and other partners to conduct
demonstrations at commercial data centers across the United States in Oregon, Chicago, and
Virginia, as well as in Europe, collaborating with partners spanning Portland General Electric,
Commonwealth Edison, Constellation Energy, PJM, and Oracle. These additional
demonstrations have showcased additional capabilities, spanning geographical shifting of AI
inference queries from Virginia to Chicago to provide relief during a winter peak period in one
region while assuring low-latency inference serving to ramping AI power use inversely with ISO
wholesale market prices to minimize energy costs and provide network congestion relief.13

These demonstrations establish that AI data centers can deliver rapid, sustained, and measurable
demand reductions in response to grid conditions. Importantly, they demonstrate that software-
defined computational flexibility can provide a distinct form of grid support, using existing
infrastructure either with or without additional batteries or on-site generation. This approach can
provide a cost-effective means of reducing electricity demand over extended periods, as
demonstrated by flexibility events lasting up to 10 hours in one Emerald AI deployment.
Together with other technologies, computational flexibility expands the range of resources
available to utilities and grid operators to maintain reliability.

 Emerald AI is also engaged with utilities and industry partners to translate these technical
capabilities into commercial-scale deployment and utility operating frameworks.

In Santa Clara, California, Emerald AI is working with Silicon Valley Power and NVIDIA
through Silicon Valley Power's Flexible Load Interconnection Program.14 Emerald AI’s
platform, operating at full data center scale, delivered 15-20% reductions in power across events
ranging from one to 24 hours in length, helping to stabilize utilities’ local network during a heat
wave and smooth out CAISO’s evening solar ramp at the peak of the “duck curve” (see
Appendix).15 The Flexible Load Interconnection Program provides a pathway for data centers to
secure expanded and accelerated grid access in exchange for verifiable, dispatchable flexibility.
Emerald AI’s software enables participating facilities to respond to utility signals during periods
of grid stress while preserving critical AI workload performance.

In Virginia, Emerald AI is also partnering with NVIDIA, Digital Realty, EPRI, PJM
Interconnection, and Dominion Energy on the NVIDIA AI Factory Research Center in
Manassas.16 This approximately 100-megawatt facility, launching in 2026, is designed to
demonstrate at commercial scale how AI computing workloads can dynamically reduce grid
demand during periods of peak system stress. This deployment will provide further evidence of
how flexible AI infrastructure can be integrated into utility and regional grid operations.

Together, these and efforts like them reflect a progression from technical validation toward
commercial deployment and the integration of flexible AI demand into utility planning and grid
operations.17

IV.     Reliability, Affordability, and Expedited Interconnection Benefits

Critically, demand flexibility does not impose tradeoffs between important FERC aims. Rather,
so long as rules are sufficiently implementable, predictable, and commercially viable, grid
reliability and consumer affordability objects are achieved. The power system must maintain

 sufficient infrastructure to serve demand during its most constrained operating periods, even
though those conditions occur relatively infrequently. As a result, substantial generation and
transmission capacity may remain underutilized during the vast majority of the year. Flexible
demand can allow additional customers to make better use of existing infrastructure while
committing to reduce consumption when the system is constrained.

Realizing these benefits requires appropriate regulatory and tariff frameworks. Interconnection
studies and service arrangements should recognize the distinction between firm demand that
must be served at all times and flexible demand that can be reduced under clearly defined system
conditions. Where flexibility provides measurable system benefits, those benefits should be
reflected in the terms under which customers obtain grid access.

 V.     Opportunities for Commission Action

The Commission has an important role in ensuring that transmission planning, interconnection
processes, and service arrangements recognize the capabilities of flexible large loads while
preserving the reliability of the bulk-power system.

First, utilities and grid operators should recognize verifiable load flexibility when evaluating
large-load interconnection requests. Data centers that commit to reducing electricity
consumption during periods of grid stress, supported by appropriate telemetry and performance
requirements, should have pathways to faster and larger grid connections.18 Incorporating these
capabilities into planning and interconnection processes would enable more efficient use of
existing infrastructure while maintaining reliability.

Second, regulatory and tariff frameworks should recognize the distinction between firm and
flexible electricity demand. Service arrangements that reflect a facility's ability to reduce
consumption during constrained periods can enable more efficient grid access and reduce the
need for costly infrastructure upgrades. These arrangements should provide clear operating
requirements and appropriate incentives for facilities that deliver reliable flexibility.

Third, these frameworks should be technology-neutral and performance-based, recognizing
flexibility delivered through computing workloads, energy storage, on-site generation, or other
technologies. Each offers different operating capabilities and costs. Software-defined
computational flexibility, in particular, should be recognized alongside other resources capable
of delivering rapid and sustained demand reductions.

And fourth, it is critical to recognize that although AI data centers can provide highly reliable
flexibility, this capability should not be overused. AI data centers are capital-intensive centers of

 economic growth that produce extremely valuable output in the form of tokens of intelligence.
These facilities can economically provide flexibility in exchange for access to faster and larger
power connections as well as revised tariffs that reflect their ability to defer or mitigate costly
infrastructure upgrades.

As the Commission, NERC, grid operators, and state regulators translate these principles into
tariffs, service agreements, and Reliability Standards, Emerald AI offers five recommendations
to ensure that every technology capable of delivering reliable flexibility can do so on equal
terms:

   ● Flexibility should be defined by measured performance. An obligation to bring grid
     withdrawals to an instructed level within a specified time, and to hold that level for a
     specified duration, gives grid operators the certainty that reliability requires while
     permitting partial reductions that keep priority workloads running. Facilities should be
     free to meet that obligation by orchestrating computing workloads, including those of
     their tenants, by drawing on batteries or on-site generation, or by coordinating these
     resources together. Equal verified performance should earn equal treatment in study
     timelines, service terms, and cost.

   ● Flexibility should be verified and verifiable, such as through revenue-grade
     metering, real-time telemetry, and periodic and unannounced testing to establish
     that a given facility reached and held its instructed level. They do so without relying
     on estimates of what the facility would otherwise have consumed or on inspection of
     particular equipment. The high-resolution monitoring that grid operators increasingly
     require at large-load interconnections can serve this purpose. Software-based workload
     orchestration should be recognized as an auditable control system whose performance
     can be tested and certified like any other.

   ● Reliability Standards for computational loads should distinguish controlled,
     instructed changes in demand from uncontrolled swings. As NERC drafts its
     standards, requirements intended to prevent sudden and unexpected changes in demand
     should accommodate rapid reductions made at the instruction of a utility or grid operator,
     along with the staged return to normal operation that follows. These intentional changes
     should be governed by clear performance expectations, such as specified ramp rates and
     coordinated recovery. That way, rules designed to contain disruptive load swings do not
     foreclose the fast response that operators also value.

   ● Grid operators and flexible facilities should communicate through standardized,
     secure, and automated interfaces. Dispatch instructions and performance data
     exchanged directly between systems, rather than through manual procedures, allow
     flexibility to be delivered within seconds to minutes and verified as it occurs. Security
     requirements for these interfaces and the control systems behind them should be risk-

        based and technology-neutral, so that well-secured software platforms can satisfy them.
       They should also build in safeguards such as authenticated commands, responses
       bounded by each facility’s committed limits, and predictable behavior if communications
       are lost.

Together, these performance standards would provide transmission providers with greater
certainty regarding the availability and reliability of flexible loads. By appropriately recognizing
and valuing flexibility, the Commission can help accommodate growing AI electricity demand,
accelerate grid connections, and make better use of existing infrastructure while protecting grid
reliability and affordability for all customers.

VI.    Conclusion

The rapid expansion of AI infrastructure presents both a significant challenge and an opportunity
for the nation's electric system. Accommodating this growth will require continued investment in
generation and transmission, improved coordination between large-load customers and grid
operators, and regulatory frameworks that reflect the evolving technical capabilities of modern
data centers.

AI data centers no longer need to be treated solely as inflexible sources of electricity demand. As
real-world demonstrations have shown, these facilities can provide rapid, sustained, and
verifiable curtailment while maintaining the performance of critical computing workloads.

By recognizing and appropriately valuing this flexibility in transmission planning,
interconnection processes, and service arrangements, the Commission can help facilitate
responsible AI infrastructure growth while protecting the reliability and affordability of
electricity service for all customers.

Emerald AI appreciates the Commission's leadership on these issues and welcomes the
opportunity to continue working with federal and state regulators, utilities, and grid operators to
advance practical, performance-based approaches to integrating flexible large loads.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide this testimony.

Respectfully submitted,
